# Part 2 — Matrix Setup and Standardization

```{python}
pred_cols = ["size_sqft", "bedrooms", "age_years"]

predictors = df[pred_cols].to_numpy()
y = df["price_thousands"].to_numpy()

means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)

Z = (predictors - means) / sds
```

Standardized columns verification of mean and standard deviation of approximately 0 and 1 respectively :

```{python}
print("Column means of Z:", np.round(Z.mean(axis=0), 3))
print("Column Standard Deviations of Z:  ", np.round(Z.std(axis=0), 3))
```

```{python}
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])
```
```{python}
pd.DataFrame(
    X[:5],
    columns=["intercept"] + pred_cols
).round(3)
```

```{python}

shape_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": [
        "Shape of Predictors", "Shape of Z", "Shape of X", "Shape of y",
        "Matrix rank of X",
        "Number of predictors",
    ],
    "Value": [
        str(predictors.shape), str(Z.shape), str(X.shape), str(y.shape),
        str(np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)),
        str(Z.shape[1]),
    ],
})
shape_table
```

`X` and `y` must have compatible shapes because each row of `X` describes
the same observation as the matching entry of `y`, so the number of rows
in `X` must equal the length of `y`. If the counts differed, some
observations would have predictors but no response, or a response but no
predictors, and the model could not compare its predictions to the data. 
Going forward, compatible shapes are also needed for the computation itself: 
`X @ beta` requires the columns of `X` to match the length of `beta`, and 
the residuals `y - X @ beta` require both vectors to have length n.


The intercept column of ones lets the model estimate a baseline
level (the predicted price when all standardized predictors are at their
means or held constant) instead of forcing the fitted surface through the origin.
Standardizing put all three predictors on a common scale with mean 0 and
standard deviation 1, so their coefficients can be compared directly.
Broadcasting makes this standardization possible without a loop because NumPy stretches
the vectors `means` and `sds`, which each contain three values (one per
predictor), across every row of the `predictors` matrix, so
`(predictors - means) / sds` is applied to each column at once bringing out the standardized matrix Z.


# Part 3 — Least squares

```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)

coef_names = ["intercept"] + [f"{c} (standardized)" for c in pred_cols]
coef_table = pd.DataFrame({"term": coef_names, "estimate": beta_hat})
coef_table
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
largest_idx = 1 + int(np.argmax(np.abs(beta_hat[1:])))
largest_name = pred_cols[largest_idx - 1]
largest_val = float(beta_hat[largest_idx])
```

The intercept is `{python} f"{beta_hat[0]:.2f}"`, which equals the mean of
`y` because the predictors are centered: it is the predicted price (in
thousands) for a house that is average on all three predictors. The
coefficient for `size_sqft` is `{python} f"{beta_hat[1]:.2f}"`, so a
one-standard-deviation increase in size is associated with a predicted
price about `{python} f"{beta_hat[1]:.2f}"` thousand higher, holding the
other predictors fixed. The coefficient for `bedrooms` is
`{python} f"{beta_hat[2]:.2f}"`, a smaller positive association, and the
coefficient for `age_years` is `{python} f"{beta_hat[3]:.2f}"`, so older
houses have lower predicted prices. Comparing absolute values, `size_sqft`
has the largest coefficient which is approximately `{python} f"{largest_val:.2f}"`, 
followed by `age_years` and then `bedrooms`.


```{python}
fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y - fitted

residuals_mean = residuals.mean()
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residuals ** 2))

print("Residual mean:", residuals.mean())
print("RMSE:", rmse)
```



`X @ beta_hat` is the matrix product of the design matrix and the
coefficient vector, so each entry is the model's fitted (predicted) price
for one house: the intercept plus each standardized predictor times its
coefficient. When an intercept is present, least squares forces the
residuals to be orthogonal to the column of ones, which means they sum to
zero, so the residual mean is near zero up to floating-point error. RMSE
summarizes the typical size of the residuals, in the same units as the
response (thousands of dollars). Finally, `X * beta_hat` multiplies element by element, broadcasting the
vector `beta_hat`, which contains four values (one per column of `X`),
down every row of `X` and returning a `{python} str(X.shape)` array, while `X @ beta_hat` does a matrix product
that sums across the columns and returns one fitted value per observation,
a `{python} str((X @ beta_hat).shape)` array which is the model's predicted price for each house, in
thousands of dollars.


# Part 4 — QR, SVD, and Conditioning

## QR Decomposition

```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)

print("Q shape:", Q.shape)
print("R shape:", R.shape)
```

### Verification of the factorization and orthonormality
```{python}
print("Q @ R ≈ X:   ", np.allclose(Q @ R, X))
print("Q.T @ Q ≈ I: ", np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1])))
```
`Q @ R ≈ X` confirms that the factorization reproduces the design matrix,
and `Q.T @ Q ≈ I` confirms that the columns of `Q` are orthonormal.



## SVD

```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)

print("U shape:", U.shape)
print("s shape:", s.shape)
print("Vt shape:", Vt.shape)
print("Singular values:", s)
```


```{python}
X_reconstructed = U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt
```

### Verification of the SVD reconstruction
```{python}
print("U S Vt ≈ X:", np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X))
```

The reconstruction `U @ diag(s) @ Vt` matches `X`, and the four singular
values (`{python} ", ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in s)`) are all well away
from zero, so no direction in the design matrix is nearly redundant.
The check `U @ diag(s) @ Vt ≈ X` returned `{python} np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X)`, so the SVD
reconstructs the design matrix.


## Rank and conditioning

```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(predictors)), predictors])

rank_X = np.linalg.matrix_rank(X)
cond_X = np.linalg.cond(X)
cond_raw = np.linalg.cond(X_raw)

pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["rank of X", "condition number of X (standardized)",
                 "condition number of X_raw (unstandardized)"],
    "Value": [str(rank_X), f"{cond_X:.3f}", f"{cond_raw:,.1f}"],
})
```


```{python}
corr = np.corrcoef(predictors, rowvar=False)
pd.DataFrame(corr, index=pred_cols, columns=pred_cols).round(2)
```



The check `Q @ R ≈ X` verifies that the QR factorization reproduces the
design matrix, and `Q.T @ Q ≈ I` verifies that the columns of `Q` are
orthonormal, which is what makes QR numerically stable for least squares.
In our results, the two checks returned `{python} np.allclose(Q @ R, X)` and
`{python} np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1]))`, so `Q @ R` reproduces `X` the design matrix and the columns of `Q` are
orthonormal. In general, singular values measure the strength of the directions in a
matrix. The singular values (`{python} ", ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in s)`) measure
the strength of the directions in `X`: large values are strong directions,
and values near zero would be weak. In the results above, `{python} ", ".join(f"{v:.2f}" for v in s)`: 
the strongest direction is `{python} f"{s[0]:.2f}"` and the weakest is `{python} f"{s[-1]:.2f}"`,
which is still about `{python} f"{s[-1] / s[0]:.0%}"` of the strongest
and far from zero, so no direction is nearly redundant.


A large condition number, the ratio of the largest to the smallest singular
value, suggests the matrix is sensitive to small perturbations, so
coefficient estimates could be unstable but the condition number of the standardized matrix
is only `{python} f"{cond_X:.2f}"`, so coefficient estimates should be
stable. The condition number dropped from
about `{python} f"{cond_raw:,.0f}"` for the raw matrix to about
`{python} f"{cond_X:.2f}"` after standardization. Measurement scale
affects the raw value because `size_sqft` is in the thousands while
`bedrooms` is a small count, so the raw columns differ hugely in
magnitude, which inflates the ratio even though the information is has not changed. The
standardized design matrix shows no evidence of severe near-redundancy,
since its smallest singular value is not close to zero and its condition
number is small. 






# Part 5 — Reproducibility and Numerical-Computing Reflection

Clean execution matters for a computational report because it ensures
that the analysis is accurate, reproducible, and reliable: anyone can
rerun the file from top to bottom and regenerate every number from the
data and code. Without it, a report can look correct while depending on
cells run out of order or values defined by hand. Rendering from a clean session 
proves that the report depends only on what is written in the file.
Reusable code should not depend on hidden notebook state because it makes the code unreliable 
and harder to reuse. If cells are executed out of order, a notebook may appear to work 
correctly while relying on values that exist only in the current session, such as a variable 
created in a cell that was later edited or deleted. Therefore, anyone running the notebook from a 
clean start may encounter errors or obtain different results. This creates reproducibility problems 
and makes the code unreliable and difficult to reuse.


In ordinary numerical work, `np.linalg.lstsq()` is preferable to manually
computing $(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$ because it is more numerically stable
and avoids explicitly calculating the inverse of a matrix. Forming
$X^\top X$ squares the condition number, and matrix inversion can amplify
numerical error. The least-squares function instead solves the problem directly 
from a stable factorization of `X`, so it gives more reliable coefficients.
Similarly, `np.allclose()` is preferable to exact equality when checking
QR and SVD reconstruction because floating-point computations lead to
small rounding errors. Even when a reconstruction is done correctly, the
computed values may differ slightly by tiny amounts. So an exact check
could show a mismatch in values even though the reconstruction is
correct. `np.allclose()` checks whether the values are sufficiently close
within specified tolerances rather than requiring exact equality.
The condition-number comparison taught me that the scale and magnitude of
data can influence numerical stability. The raw design matrix had a
condition number of about `{python} f"{cond_raw:,.0f}"`, compared with
`{python} f"{cond_X:.2f}"` after standardization, because variables
measured on very different scales can produce poorly conditioned
matrices, making numerical calculations more sensitive to small errors.
A large condition number therefore does not by itself show that
predictors are redundant, so examining condition numbers is an important
diagnostic practice that should be read alongside the singular values
when considering whether rescaling variables is necessary.


One practice I will carry into the final project is rendering the whole
report from a clean session with `quarto render` before submitting. This
will help me confirm that all required variables are defined, functions
are self-contained, and results do not depend on any hidden notebook state. Ultimately,
these practices will make my final project more reliable, transparent, and
reproducible.
